title: The Connected Sayings
hook: thousands of short discourses gathered by topic

segments.voice: Yesterday: the short books closed, and your line, short and deep. Which line stayed with you? Today a new block begins, and a very different kind of book: thousands of discourses, sorted like a library. Day six hundred thirty-six.

A hardware store doesn't shelve things by size. Hinges go with hinges, nails with nails, paint with paint, big or small. Walk in needing one little bracket and you know which aisle to try. The early Buddhist community had thousands of short teachings to remember, and at some point someone sorted a great many of them into aisles by topic. That sorted store is the third great collection of the Pali canon. Today: the Samyutta Nikaya.
screen: `A HARDWARE STORE.` → `SORTED BY KIND, NOT SIZE.` → `THOUSANDS OF TEACHINGS, BY TOPIC.`

segments.voice: Samyutta means connected, or yoked together, and nikaya means a collection. So the Connected Sayings: discourses yoked together by their subject. The Long Discourses were sorted by length. The Middle-Length, more or less by length too. The Samyutta is sorted by kind. All the conversations with devas go in one chapter. All the meetings with Mara in another. The talks with King Pasenadi together, the teachings on feeling together, on the five heaps, on the six senses, on the path. There are fifty-six of these chapters, gathered into five books. The first book is the one with verses, full of short poems and questions from gods, kings and nuns. The others take on the great themes: how things arise from causes, the heaps, the senses, and finally the path and the four noble truths. Many of the discourses are tiny, a few lines, sometimes just a simile. That's what makes the collection so useful to read slowly. Here's one, paraphrased, from the chapter on breakthrough. The Buddha picks up a little dust on the tip of his fingernail and asks the monks: which is more, this dust or the great earth? The earth, sir, of course. The dust is nothing beside it. In the same way, he says, for a disciple who has truly seen the teaching, the suffering already ended is like the earth. What's left is like the dust on a fingernail. That's the whole discourse. The Connected Sayings are full of moments like that, small, sorted, and easy to find again. For the next weeks, we'll walk the aisles one at a time.
screen: `SAMYUTTA: YOKED TOGETHER` · `SORTED BY KIND, NOT LENGTH` · `FIFTY-SIX CHAPTERS, FIVE BOOKS` · `DUST ON A FINGERNAIL` · then, large: `GATHERED BY KIND.`

segments.voice: Here's a short discourse to read with the body. Hold up one hand and look at a fingernail. Imagine a few grains of dust on its tip. Then let the mind open out to the ground under you, the street, the land, the whole earth. Feel the difference in size. Now think of a difficulty you've already come through in life, something that once felt enormous and is behind you. Let it be the earth. Whatever is still hard today, let it, for now, be the dust. Rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Samyutta Nikaya. The Connected Sayings: thousands of short discourses, yoked together by topic into fifty-six chapters and five books. Today's word.
Your line: gathered by kind. Read one short discourse today, from any book you like, and notice which aisle it would belong in. Day six hundred thirty-six.

howItsDone: Theravada monastics and lay students study the Samyutta Nikaya chapter by chapter, and teachers draw short similes from it for talks, since its discourses are grouped by topic.

original.note: Pali Samyutta Nikaya: the collection of connected, yoked-together discourses.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Connected Sayings are sayings that link to each other in a story.
what it means: thousands of short discourses gathered by topic into fifty-six chapters and five books.
what a scholar hears: the Samyutta has a close counterpart preserved in Chinese translation, the Samyuktagama, also arranged by topic.

notes: Block F opens. Confirm: 56 samyuttas in five vaggas (Sagatha, Nidana, Khandha, Salayatana, Maha); 'third great collection' follows the usual order DN, MN, SN, AN.

SN 13.1 (Abhisamaya Samyutta, the fingernail) paraphrased; confirm the simile (a little dust on the fingernail versus the great earth; for a noble disciple accomplished in view, the suffering destroyed is far greater than what remains, at most seven more lives).
The Chinese Samyuktagama parallel is a standard scholarly note.
The Middle-Length Discourses being 'more or less by length' is a simplification; a Keeper may prefer different wording.
